title: 09. Storage, CDN & Data Engineering: Data Lake
summary: A data lake is a centralized storage repository that holds structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale, ingested as-is from source systems with the schema applied later at read time (schema-on-read),…
objectives: What is the difference between schema-on-write and schema-on-read, and why does the data lake prefer the latter?
What are the data lake zones, and why are they separated?
What is the "data swamp" anti-pattern, and how do you avoid it?
What is a lakehouse, and how does it differ from a data lake?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A data lake is a centralized storage repository that holds structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data at any scale, ingested as-is from source systems with the schema applied later at read time (schema-on-read), enabling exploratory analytics, machine learning, and downstream ETL into a warehouse without forcing an upfront model on the data.

A data lake is the architectural answer to a question that became unavoidable in the 2010s: where do you put the data you don't yet know how to use? A traditional data warehouse requires you to define a schema before you load data — columns, types, partitions, dimensions, facts — and any source that doesn't fit the model is rejected or transformed on the way in. That works well for sales reports and financial summaries, where the questions are known and stable, but it breaks down when you have clickstreams with new event types every week, IoT sensors emitting JSON with evolving fields, mobile app logs in proprietary binary formats, customer support transcripts as free text, and machine learning training data as images and audio. The data lake says: store everything first, ask questions later. Pour all your raw sources — CSV, JSON, Parquet, Avro, ORC, images, video, audio, binary blobs — into a single object store or distributed filesystem, organize them by source and ingestion date, and let analysts, data scientists, and ML engineers figure out the schema when they actually read the data.

The architectural pattern is a layered, zone-based storage model. The canonical layout, popularized by Netflix and Uber, has three or four zones stacked vertically on the same underlying storage. The **raw zone** (also called "landing" or "bronze") receives data exactly as it arrived from source systems — no transformation, no validation, no schema enforcement — preserving the original bytes with a partition like `dt=2024-03-15/source=kafka`. The **curated zone** (also called "conformance" or "silver") holds cleaned, deduplicated, type-cast data in an open columnar format (Parquet or ORC) with a defined schema, ready for SQL queries and BI tools. The **consumption zone** (also called "gold" or "mart") holds business-level aggregates and feature stores, often materialized as Parquet tables registered in a metastore like Hive Metastore, AWS Glue, or a Delta/Iceberg catalog. An optional **sandbox zone** gives data scientists a scratch space for exploratory analysis without polluting the curated zone. The boundaries between zones are enforced by ETL pipelines — typically Spark, dbt, or Airflow-orchestrated jobs — that read from the raw zone, transform, and write to the curated zone, with schema validation at the boundary.

The defining trade-off of a data lake is flexibility-over-discipline. Schema-on-read means you can ingest anything in minutes — a new event type, a new partner's CSV, a new sensor's JSON — without coordinating with a data modeling team. But it also means the lake can quickly fill with low-quality, undocumented, duplicative data — what the industry famously calls a "data swamp." A table in the raw zone might have 200 fields, 150 of which are null, 30 of which are duplicates from a botched migration, and 10 of which have changed meaning three times in the past year. Without strong cataloging (AWS Glue, DataHub, Amundsen, Atlas), lineage tracking (OpenLineage, Spline), and access controls (Apache Ranger, Lake Formation), the lake becomes unsearchable and untrustworthy. The discipline required is operational, not storage: every dataset needs an owner, a description, a schema, and a freshness SLA; every pipeline needs lineage so analysts can trace a metric back to its source; every access needs audit logging for compliance. Netflix's famous "data platform as a product" philosophy treats the data lake like an internal product with users, SLAs, and on-call rotations, not a dumping ground.

The real-world example is Netflix's S3 data lake, which by 2020 held more than 100 PB of data across billions of objects in S3, organized by source (playback events, billing, content metadata, A/B test results, ML features). Every Netflix playback event — every play, pause, seek, and error from 200+ million subscribers — lands as JSON in an S3 raw zone within seconds via Kafka and Kinesis Firehose. Spark jobs on EMR read the raw zone, parse the JSON, and write curated Parquet tables partitioned by date and content ID. Analysts query those tables with Presto/Trino ( federated SQL over S3), data scientists train recommendation models on feature stores materialized in S3, and dashboards in Tableau and Looker aggregate to daily metrics. The lake's value is that the same raw event can serve dozens of downstream uses — billing reconciliation, content recommendation, anomaly detection, capacity planning — without each consumer needing to coordinate with the ingestion pipeline. Uber's Hadoop data lake tells a similar story: every trip event, every restaurant order, every support ticket flows into an S3/HDFS lake, and hundreds of Spark and Presto jobs transform it into the tables that power surge pricing, fraud detection, and driver payouts.

The modern data lake has evolved into the "lakehouse" architecture, which adds warehouse-like transactional semantics on top of the lake's cheap storage. The three open table formats — Delta Lake (from Databricks), Apache Iceberg (from Netflix, now widely adopted), and Apache Hudi (from Uber) — provide ACID transactions, schema enforcement, time travel, and upserts on top of Parquet files in S3. A Delta/Iceberg/Hudi table is a set of Parquet files plus a metadata log (in Delta's case, a JSON transaction log; in Iceberg's, an Avro manifest list) that tracks which files are part of which snapshot, allowing a reader to see a consistent point-in-time view even as writers are appending and updating. This combines the lake's flexibility (open format, cheap storage, ML-friendly) with the warehouse's guarantees (ACID, schema, time travel), and is the architectural direction most new data platforms are taking. The cost model is favorable: S3 Standard at $0.023/GB-month for hot data, lifecycle to S3 IA at $0.0125 after 30 days, and Glacier Deep Archive at $0.00099/GB-month for cold data — meaning a 100 PB lake can be operated for under $2M/month in storage, with compute (Spark, Presto, EMR) as the dominant cost on top.

Scheduled Spark or dbt jobs read from the raw zone, apply schema (parse JSON to typed columns, cast, deduplicate, validate), and write Parquet to the curated zone with a registered schema in the metastore; Delta/Iceberg/Hudi add ACID and time travel on top. 3. sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Mini data-lake mock: zone-based storage (raw / curated / gold) over an in-memory S3-like store.
- Tracks tables, schemas, lineage (like AWS Glue or Hive Metastore).
- Dump records as JSONL into the raw zone.
- Read raw JSONL, parse, type-cast, write Parquet-ish to curated.
- Raw zone: ingest as-is, schema-on-read
- Raw zone has NO schema enforced - schema-on-read means
- Analysts apply schema when they query, not when we ingest.
- Curated zone: ETL parses raw, enforces schema

**Defines:** `ObjectStore`, `TableMeta`, `Metastore`, `DataLake`

```python
"""
Mini data-lake mock: zone-based storage (raw / curated / gold) over an
in-memory S3-like store. Demonstrates schema-on-read, ETL between zones,
and a tiny metastore that tracks schema + lineage.
"""
import json, time, uuid
from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from typing import Any

# ------------------------- S3-like object store -------------------------
class ObjectStore:
    """Pretend S3. Keyed by s3://bucket/prefix/key -> bytes."""
    def __init__(self):
        self._objects: dict[str, bytes] = {}
    def put(self, key: str, data: bytes):
        self._objects[key] = data
    def get(self, key: str) -> bytes:
        return self._objects[key]
    def list(self, prefix: str) -> list[str]:
        return sorted(k for k in self._objects if k.startswith(prefix))

# ------------------------- Metastore (catalog) --------------------------
@dataclass
class TableMeta:
    name: str
    zone: str                       # 'raw' | 'curated' | 'gold'
    location: str                   # s3:// prefix
    schema: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)   # col -> type
    partitions: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    lineage: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)       # upstream tables
    created_at: float = time.time()

class Metastore:
    """Tracks tables, schemas, lineage (like AWS Glue or Hive Metastore)."""
    def __init__(self):
        self.tables: dict[str, TableMeta] = {}
    def register(self, meta: TableMeta):
        self.tables[meta.name] = meta
    def get(self, name: str) -> TableMeta:
        return self.tables[name]
    def lineage_of(self, name: str) -> list[str]:
        return self.tables[name].lineage

# ------------------------- Data Lake -------------------------------------
class DataLake:
    def __init__(self):
        self.s3 = ObjectStore()
        self.catalog = Metastore()
        # Pre-create zone prefixes
        for zone in ["raw", "curated", "gold"]:
            self.s3.put(f"s3://lake/{zone}/.zone_marker", b"")

    # ---- Raw zone: ingest as-is, schema-on-read ----
    def ingest_raw(self, source: str, dt: str, records: list[dict]):
        """Dump records as JSONL into the raw zone. No transformation."""
        path = f"s3://lake/raw/{source}/dt={dt}/data.jsonl"
        payload = "\n".join(json.dumps(r) for r in records).encode()
        self.s3.put(path, payload)
        # Raw zone has NO schema enforced - schema-on-read means
        # analysts apply schema when they query, not when we ingest.
        tbl = f"raw_{source}"
        if tbl not in self.catalog.tables:
            self.catalog.register(TableMeta(
                name=tbl, zone="raw", location=f"s3://lake/raw/{source}/",
                schema={"(schema-on-read)": "various"},
                partitions=["dt"], lineage=[f"source:{source}"]))
        print(f"  ingested {len(records)} records -> {path}")
        return path

    # ---- Curated zone: ETL parses raw, enforces schema ----
    def etl_to_curated(self, source: str, dt: str, schema: dict[str, str]):
        """Read raw JSONL, parse, type-cast, write Parquet-ish to curated."""
        raw_path = f"s3://lake/raw/{source}/dt={dt}/data.jsonl"
        if not self.s3.list(raw_path):
            raise FileNotFoundError(raw_path)
        raw_records = [json.loads(l) for l in
                       self.s3.get(raw_path).decode().splitlines()]
        # Apply schema: keep only declared columns, cast types
        curated = []
        for r in raw_records:
            row = {}
            for col, typ in schema.items():
                if col in r:
                    row[col] = self._cast(r[col], typ)
                else:
                    row[col] = None  # missing -> null
            curated.append(row)
        out_path = f"s3://lake/curated/{source}/dt={dt}/data.parquet"
        # (Real Parquet is columnar binary; we store JSON for the demo.)
        self.s3.put(out_path, json.dumps(curated).encode())
        tbl = f"curated_{source}"
        upstream = f"raw_{source}"
        self.catalog.register(TableMeta(
            name=tbl, zone="curated", location=f"s3://lake/curated/{source}/",
            schema=schema, partitions=["dt"], lineage=[upstream]))
        print(f"  ETL: raw_{source} -> curated_{source} "
              f"({len(curated)} rows, schema enforced)")
        return out_path

    def _cast(self, val: Any, typ: str) -> Any:
        try:
            if typ == "int":    return int(val)
            if typ == "float":  return float(val)
            if typ == "string": return str(val)
            if typ == "bool":   return bool(val)
        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            return None
        return val

    # ---- Gold zone: business aggregates ----
    def aggregate_to_gold(self, source: str, dt: str,
                          group_by: str, agg_col: str, agg_fn: str):
        """Group curated rows and compute an aggregate -> gold table."""
        cur_path = f"s3://lake/curated/{source}/dt={dt}/data.parquet"
        rows = json.loads(self.s3.get(cur_path).decode())
        groups: dict[Any, list] = {}
        for r in rows:
            groups.setdefault(r.get(group_by), []).append(r.get(agg_col))
        result = []
        for k, vals in groups.items():
            if agg_fn == "sum":
                v = sum(x for x in vals if x is not None)
            elif agg_fn == "count":
                v = len(vals)
            elif agg_fn == "avg":
                nums = [x for x in vals if x is not None]
                v = sum(nums) / len(nums) if nums else None
            else:
                raise ValueError(agg_fn)
            result.append({group_by: k, agg_col: v})
        gold_path = f"s3://lake/gold/{source}_by_{group_by}/dt={dt}/data.parquet"
        self.s3.put(gold_path, json.dumps(result).encode())
        tbl = f"gold_{source}_by_{group_by}"
        self.catalog.register(TableMeta(
            name=tbl, zone="gold",
            location=f"s3://lake/gold/{source}_by_{group_by}/",
            schema={group_by: "string", agg_col: "float"},
            partitions=["dt"],
            lineage=[f"curated_{source}"]))
        print(f"  Aggregate: curated_{source} -> {tbl} ({len(result)} groups)")
        return gold_path

    # ---- Schema-on-read query ----
    def query_raw(self, source: str, dt: str,
                  select: list[str], where: callable = None) -> list[dict]:
        """Schema-on-read: apply projection/filter at query time, not ingest."""
        raw_path = f"s3://lake/raw/{source}/dt={dt}/data.jsonl"
        if not self.s3.list(raw_path):
            return []
        rows = [json.loads(l) for l in self.s3.get(raw_path).decode().splitlines()]
        if where:
            rows = [r for r in rows if where(r)]
        return [{c: r.get(c) for c in select} for r in rows]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    lake = DataLake()

    # --- 1. Ingest raw clickstream events (schema-on-read) ---
    print("=== Ingest raw clickstream ===")
    events = [
        {"user_id": "u1", "event": "click", "url": "/home", "ts": 1, "amount": 0},
        {"user_id": "u2", "event": "click", "url": "/buy",  "ts": 2, "amount": 49},
        {"user_id": "u1", "event": "click", "url": "/buy",  "ts": 3, "amount": 12},
        {"user_id": "u3", "event": "scroll", "url": "/home", "ts": 4, "amount": 0},
        {"user_id": "u2", "event": "click", "url": "/buy",  "ts": 5, "amount": 99},
    ]
    lake.ingest_raw("clicks", "2024-03-15", events)

    # --- 2. ETL: raw -> curated (schema enforced) ---
    print("\n=== ETL raw -> curated ===")
    lake.etl_to_curated("clicks", "2024-03-15", schema={
        "user_id": "string", "event": "string",
        "url": "string", "amount": "float",
    })

    # --- 3. Aggregate: curated -> gold (revenue by user) ---
    print("\n=== Aggregate curated -> gold ===")
    lake.aggregate_to_gold("clicks", "2024-03-15",
                           group_by="user_id", agg_col="amount", agg_fn="sum")

    # --- 4. Schema-on-read: query raw directly (no schema needed) ---
    print("\n=== Schema-on-read query on raw ===")
    results = lake.query_raw("clicks", "2024-03-15",
                             select=["user_id", "url"],
                             where=lambda r: r.get("event") == "click")
    for r in results:
        print(" ", r)

    # --- 5. Lineage check ---
    print("\n=== Lineage ===")
    print("gold_clicks_by_user_id <-", lake.catalog.lineage_of("gold_clicks_by_user_id"))
    print("curated_clicks <-",        lake.catalog.lineage_of("curated_clicks"))
```

Symptoms include analysts spending 80% of their time hunting for data and verifying its quality, duplicate tables with conflicting numbers, and pipelines failing silently.
